reader.title: Ambush of Mexican traders at Las Animas, Sonora
bases: A band of about twenty cowboys ambushed and robbed a party of Mexican traders in Sonora, with no accusation, custody or claim of justice (A1, A2, A5).
Twenty cowboys fired on the traders illegally and four or five were supposed killed (A1, A2, A5), but the attack was a robbery from ambush with no pretext of justice, race or tradition reported.
Every report traces to second-hand 'Sonora news' relayed from Tucson (A1, A2, A5); the wire and the Citizen agree on the ambush and robbery but no independent account confirms any death.

summary.text: The ambush of Mexican traders at Las Animas was an attack by cowboys on a party of Mexican traders camped at Las Animas, near Fronteras in Sonora, Mexico, on the morning of July 26, 1881.
The traders fled, leaving their mules, pack saddles and $4,000, and four or five of them were reported missing and supposed killed.
Carried east by a Tucson dispatch, the story ran in papers from New York to Montana and was later cited as evidence of lawlessness on the Arizona border.
According to the reports, the party came from the interior of Sonora and was travelling to Arizona to buy goods, carrying $4,000 for the purpose.
The Tucson Citizen put the party at sixteen men.
The traders had stopped at a curve in the road at Las Animas, which the Citizen spelled "Los Animas," to cook breakfast.
While they were "preparing their tortillas," about twenty cowboys lying in ambush opened fire on them.
The Mexicans ran, abandoning their mules and the pack saddles that held their money, which were left "as plunder to the cowboys."
How many died was never settled in the coverage.
The "Sonora news" relayed from Tucson said that when the party reached Fronteras four men were missing, and they were believed killed.
The wire dispatch sent through San Francisco said instead that five Mexicans were "supposed to have been killed."

Reports said a large force of Mexican troops set out after the cowboys, and the Citizen added that the citizens of Babispe had joined them and were "disposed to take summary vengeance" if they caught the attackers.
No report of an arrest, of the attackers being overtaken, or of the missing men being found appears in the coverage.
Weeks later a syndicated news brief said that Arizona's civil authorities "seem powerless" and that the Mexicans held "the Americans responsible for the outrages."
All the coverage came from white papers, and all of it traced back to Tucson.

A short wire item dated at San Francisco on August 1 and 2 reached the Helena Weekly Herald, the New-York Tribune under the headline "Mexicans Killed by Cowboys," and the Wilmington Daily Republican, which ran it in a "Deeds of Violence" column and called the cowboys "the murderers."

Reprints followed through mid-August in the Savannah Morning News, the Martinsburg Independent, the Somerset Herald ("Ambushed and Killed"), the Benton Weekly Record ("Ambushed by Cowboys") and the Narragansett Herald.

Closer to the border, the Tucson Citizen's account, reprinted by the Weekly Arizona Miner under the headline "An Interrupted Breakfast," called the attack "a fresh outrage perpetrated by the cowboys in Sonora" but told it as a joke.
It described the gunfire as "the music of twenty rifles" and said the Mexicans "took this as an invitation to leave."

Later in August a syndicated brief gave four dead and $5,000 taken, and an editorial paragraph in the Cairo Bulletin cited a Sonora train robbed by "Arizona cow-boys" as the start of "guerrilla work" on the border that "demands prompt attention on the part of the United States."
The number of dead differs by source: five "supposed" killed in the wire, four missing and believed killed in the Sonora news and the Citizen, and four killed outright in the later brief.
The Citizen's count rests on the men missing when the party reached Fronteras, while the wire gives no basis for its five.
The Citizen also dated the attack to "last Monday," whereas the other Tucson reports gave the 26th, a Tuesday.
The Cairo Bulletin's version, with two killed and the train bound for Tombstone, gives no place or date and may describe a different robbery.

accounts.label: Tucson wire (via San Francisco)
accounts.gist: Traders ambushed by cowboys July 26 near Las Animas while eating breakfast; five supposed killed; pack train and $4,000 left; Mexican troops in pursuit.

accounts.label: Sonora news relayed from Tucson; Tucson Citizen
accounts.gist: Sixteen traders attacked by twenty cowboys in ambush at a curve in the road near Fronteras; four were missing at Fronteras and supposed killed; citizens of Babispe and troops in pursuit.

accounts.label: Later news-in-brief
accounts.gist: A band of cowboys killed four of a Sonora caravan and carried off $5,000; Mexicans blamed the Americans and Arizona's civil authorities 'seem powerless'.

accounts.label: Cairo Bulletin editorial paragraph
accounts.gist: A Mexican train from Sonora bound for Tombstone was robbed by Arizona cowboys and two of its men killed, followed by a Mexican retaliation on American butchers.

framing.detail: Eastern and Western papers ran the Tucson wire under 'Mexicans Killed by Cowboys', 'Ambushed and Killed' and 'Ambushed by Cowboys', some calling the cowboys 'the murderers'.
The Tucson Citizen called it a 'fresh outrage' by cowboys but told it in mocking terms ('An Interrupted Breakfast', 'saluted with the music of twenty rifles', 'their frugal breakfast').
Later paragraphs treated it as part of border 'outrages' and 'guerrilla work' needing federal attention.

versions.value: Four missing on reaching Fronteras, believed killed
Two killed (a train bound for Tombstone, possibly a different attack)

conflicts.note: The Sonora/Citizen version explains its count (four missing at Fronteras), and the wire's five is unexplained; no report confirms any death.
July 26, 1881 fell on a Tuesday; the Citizen's original publication date is not in the coverage, so its 'last Monday' cannot be fixed.
The $5,000 figure appears only in the later syndicated brief.
